report:
**Conclusion: The claim is supported by evidence — bystander hands-only CPR IS associated with greater survival after OHCA than no bystander CPR.**

The evidence consistently shows that any bystander CPR, including hands-only (compression-only) CPR, improves survival compared to no bystander CPR:

- A Swedish review of OHCA data found that "the chance of survival was doubled for any form of CPR compared with no CPR" and that compression-only CPR increased six-fold over 18 years, contributing to improved outcomes (https://www.emergency-live.com/health-and-safety/survive-an-ohca-the-american-heart-association-revealed-that-hands-only-cpr-increases-survival-rate/).

- A multivariable-adjusted observational study concluded that "both types of bystander CPR were associated with higher survival, as compared to patients with no bystander CPR" (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9803815/).

- A 2025 PubMed study states: "Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) for out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) is associated with higher survival" and examined time-to-bystander-CPR thresholds compared to no bystander CPR (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40015622/).

- The American Heart Association reports that "CPR, especially if performed immediately, can double or triple a cardiac arrest victim's chance of survival" and that hands-only CPR is as effective as conventional CPR in the first few minutes (https://cpr.heart.org/en/resources/cpr-facts-and-stats).

The evidence does not support the view that the claim is false. Multiple observational studies and reviews demonstrate that bystander hands-only CPR is associated with significantly greater survival than no bystander CPR after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.
